state: The Feature Registry resolves a feature name to an immutable configuration record. The Registry Index checks its in-memory map, and the Remote Overlay Store may contain a newer revision for the same name. A lookup may legitimately find nothing: a feature can be disabled, not yet deployed, or intentionally absent from the overlay. The Feature Resolver needs to distinguish that ordinary absence from a malformed remote document, a timeout, and an authorization failure, since only the last three require diagnostics and retry behavior. When no record exists, the caller may apply a documented default and continue rendering the application. The current implementation returns null, which caused the Notification Center to dereference it and the Metrics Collector to count the absence as a successful zero-valued setting. Define the contract across Registry Index, Remote Overlay Store, Feature Resolver, Notification Center, and Metrics Collector so absence is explicit at every call site, while failures that require investigation still expose their reason and cannot be mistaken for a missing feature.

Two enhancers must combine, with authorization receiving the tenant supplied by the other enhancer. Existing base components must remain unaware of the permission service and must work unchanged when the enhancement is not installed.

state: The RuleKit service lets operations teams write policies such as "permit if tenant.acl contains owner and request.amount < limit". Its Lexer emits tokens, the PolicyParser builds a syntax tree, and PolicyEvaluator executes that tree. The grammar has ordered alternatives, repetitions, nested parenthesized terms, and left-recursive expression forms such as amount < limit and limit <= amount. The team forbids generated parser artifacts because policy syntax changes weekly and the production build has no code-generation stage. It also requires clear stack traces that identify the exact grammar production and input token, and the parser must make one forward pass without speculative rescanning. Engineering must decide how to organize parsing so that alternatives are selected with the available lookahead, repetitions become loops, and the expression grammar can still be represented without recursive calls that never return. The resulting tree remains consumed only by PolicyEvaluator and the policy formatter.

state: A cooperative harbor game contains patrolling guards, animated statues, homing projectiles, and crowd agents. Each actor type has its own recurring behavior: GuardPatrol chooses a route, StatueCharge accumulates energy, ProjectileMotion steers toward a target, and CrowdAgent selects a local goal. The central FrameDriver currently contains type checks and inline blocks for all four behaviors, making it difficult to add an actor without editing the driver. Each live participant must advance exactly once per simulation tick, in a deterministic registry order, and newly spawned actors must not be advanced twice in the same tick. A behavior must also be able to request removal without invalidating the current traversal. Input polling and presentation must continue while actors advance, and no actor may run an unbounded private loop that prevents other actors from progressing. The design must establish a clear home for actor-specific recurring behavior and a uniform way for the driver to invoke it across heterogeneous object types.

state: A document search page contains a search input, an inline suggestion preview, a validation message, a clear button, and a results table elsewhere on the page. The query text is currently stored at the page level even though only the input, its local validation, and its preview consume it. Every keystroke invalidates the entire page, and unit tests must initialize unrelated page state to exercise the search field. The results table does not need the raw query because it receives an already resolved result set. A separate results-layout control is shared by several pages and only accepts pagination and result metadata. The field implementation should own its text, validation result, and preview projection, while the shared control remains reusable with literal, server, and test data. A framework-provided local reactive value is acceptable if it preserves that narrow ownership.

state: PaperLoop is a cloud manuals service. Deployment is 12 machines running thousands of lightweight isolated processes that never share memory. Each process owns private state plus a mailbox and handles one immutable envelope at a time, sent by address with no direct calls. EdgeIngress processes receive client edits and send them on. A DocShard process per open manual holds a private tree of Paragraph, ImageFrame, GridBlock and EmbedClip nodes. A Guardian supervisor starts and monitors EdgeIngress and a ShardSupervisor; ShardSupervisor starts, watches and restarts shards, and shards can move between machines with senders unaware. ExportPool and AuditPool are groups of similar processes that build outputs from tree snapshots mailed to them and reply with results. The node kinds are stable but work over them keeps growing: HTML export, PDF export, word totals, compliance checks, accessibility audits, plus new customer analyses each quarter. Today each new analysis adds a method to all four node classes, mixing formatting, legal and counting concerns into the model and forcing rebuild and redeploy of a core library owned by another team. Product requires new analyses to ship without edits to those four classes and without disturbing live shards.

state: ParcelNow operates a metro same-day delivery mesh. IntakeGateway validates customer orders and emits immutable order records. Each city district runs a DistrictCoordinator that holds private queue and routing state, and each courier is mirrored by a CourierUnit that holds private position, capacity and shift state. No unit shares memory; all coordination happens by sending immutable records such as OrderOffered, BidSubmitted and RouteAssigned to queue addresses, processed one message at a time. Supervising parents restart crashed children and routing is location-transparent, so units migrate across six Kubernetes nodes under bursty lunch and evening peaks. Fare logic lives inside DistrictCoordinator message handling: bike versus van versus e-cargo pricing, downtown surge multipliers, suburban flat fees, and corporate subscription discounts are branched with nested ifs. Product adds or tweaks a city rule almost weekly and ops wants to flip rules per district and time window without redeploy or pausing message flow. The handler has grown to 900 lines, unit tests need a full coordinator with queues to check one formula, and a missed branch overcharged corporate orders last month.

state: ParcelFlow runs as a cluster of small private-state processes spread over six machines. Each process owns its memory, keeps an inbox queue, and never touches another process memory or invokes its methods directly; all coordination happens by placing small records into inboxes and resuming when replies arrive. Placement is location transparent and a supervision tree restarts crashed processes from snapshots. OrderIntake receives buy requests. To admit one it needs three separate confirmations: StockKeeper holds counts per warehouse, RiskScorer grades payment trust from recent history, AddressChecker confirms deliverability against a carrier feed. Each keeper lives on different nodes and answers only through queued dispatches with timeouts and retries. Today OrderIntake chains the three lookups one after another, feeding the reply of one into the request for the next even though all inputs are known up front from the buy request, so latency adds up and the buyer sees only the first rejection. Product requires p95 admission under 250ms, at most one outbound request per keeper per buy, independent checks to overlap in time, and a single response that lists every failed check with field level reasons so the storefront can fix all problems at once. Peaks reach 4k buys per minute, replies may arrive in any order, and late or duplicate replies must not corrupt pending admissions.

state: PayShield operates a payment screening service built around a fleet of versioned predictors. Event Collector ingests authorization requests and forwards them to Feature Builder, which joins streaming card signals with a Feature Store. Live Scoring Cluster loads the current predictor artifact from Predictor Registry onto accelerator-backed pods and returns hold, release or step-up with a fee quote. Training Orchestrator retrains nightly on labeled chargebacks from Feedback Loop and promotes challengers after Evaluation Harness passes. Chargeback Auditor and Merchant Billing must replay why a past transaction was held and what fee applied. Today Fee Table and Predictor Release rows keep only current thresholds and a last_modified stamp. Product cannot stage a fee change for next month without an overnight cutover job, Risk cannot answer which thresholds were authoritative for a March dispute, and a back-dated correction overwrites what auditors saw. The team needs a design where each fee schedule and each promoted predictor carries its own start and end dates, so any read can be evaluated as of the transaction instant, future rows can be entered ahead of time, and corrections create new dated rows instead of mutating history.

state: Meridian runs a personalization service whose revenue path is serving versioned ranking checkpoints. EdgeReceiver accepts tenant HTTP requests and emits interaction events to FeatureLedger, which builds point-in-time feature frames from streaming and batch sources. ForgeScheduler schedules distributed training jobs on a GPU cluster and publishes weight bundles with metrics to VaultRegistry, the versioned store of record. ServePool is an autoscaled fleet of inference workers that boot from a pinned bundle in VaultRegistry, support canary redeploys, and must score each homepage request within 45ms p99. EvalHarness replays held-out frames to gate promotion or rollback. Tenant, corpus snapshot, trial run, and checkpoint revision are all 36-char UUID strings passed through shared Python helpers for Postgres lookup, LRU caching, structured logging, and routing. Two outages swapped corpus and checkpoint arguments during warmup and routed one tenant corpus into another tenant scoring path, serving stale weights for six hours. Any change must keep Postgres and JSON payloads as plain strings, add no measurable cost to scoring, and preserve the external REST contract.

state: ShopSphere runs a personalized offers platform where request revenue flows through learned predictors. CatalogIngest feeds FeatureLedger, nightly jobs publish versioned checkpoints to CheckpointRegistry, and an InferenceFleet serves CandidateRanker and WillingnessToPayEstimator behind InferenceGateway with autoscaled GPU pools, canary rollout via ExperimentRouter, and rollback on drift alarms from QualityMonitor. OfferComposer calls the fleet per shopper request to select items and attach tailored discounts, then CheckoutGateway settles orders. Inside this flow, BasketPricer in Python owns quote logic. Its BasketCalculator exposes process(items), applyStuff(flag), getTotal() and setRate(x). Calls mutate a running total field, read a global promo switch, pull FX rates over the network, and append audit rows to a shared table. The same basket yields different totals across calls and tests must boot the fleet, ledger and DB to reproduce a number. Discount, tax and rebate rules are reused for validation at checkout and for offline simulation, but call sites copy adjustment sequences by hand. The team must decide how to reorganize this calculation surface so repeated quotes are reproducible and testable without the surrounding services.

state: Trailhead Outdoors serves two clients: TrailX Mobile on iOS and Android and TrailX Web portal built as a React SPA. All mobile calls go only to MobileEdge and all web calls go only to WebEdge. Each edge exposes different shapes for the same downstream InventoryService, PricingService and OrderService: MobileEdge compresses lists, aggregates telemetry and trims images while WebEdge returns full detail views. MobileEdge and WebEdge deploy as separate containers with separate autoscaling groups and release trains so mobile aggregation can evolve without touching web. Inside MobileEdge, HTTP worker threads accept frequent location pings and place them into a shared in-memory BatchQueue capped at 5000 entries; a pool of sender threads removes batches and forwards them to AnalyticsService. Under burst load concurrent puts and takes interleave, corrupting head, tail and count and losing pings, while sleep-retry in handlers and tight polling in senders waste CPU and inflate p99 latency. When the queue is full handlers must pause without dropping data until space frees; when empty senders must pause without spinning until work arrives. WebEdge does not share this queue.

state: ShopSphere runs two storefronts: ShopSphere Mobile on iOS and Android, and ShopSphere Web SPA on desktop. Mobile clients call only MobileEdge, a Python FastAPI service that authenticates mobile sessions, fetches from CatalogService, PricingService, InventoryService and RecommenderService, and returns compact payloads with resized images. Web clients call only WebEdge, a separate Python FastAPI service that authenticates web sessions, fetches from the same four downstreams, and returns larger desktop payloads with extra merchandising fields. The two edge services deploy and scale independently and neither serves the other frontend. MobileEdge runs 96 workers sharing a single outbound HTTP pool of 80 connections for all downstream calls. During the last sale RecommenderService p99 rose to 9 seconds while inventory and pricing stayed under 120ms. MobileEdge workers piled up waiting on recommender calls, the shared pool filled with long waits, and checkout requests needing only inventory and pricing waited behind recommender work and then errored. WebEdge stayed healthy. Product requires that a slowdown in one downstream must not starve unrelated calls inside MobileEdge even if the slowdown lasts minutes, without adding new infrastructure.

state: ShopMobileEdge and ShopWebEdge are two independently deployable gateway services in front of shared CatalogService, PricingService and InventoryService. Native iOS and Android apps send HTTPS only to ShopMobileEdge, which trims payloads and aggregates catalog plus pricing plus stock into compact mobile responses. The React browser app sends HTTPS only to ShopWebEdge, which aggregates the same downstream services into verbose desktop responses with recommendations and larger images. Each gateway has its own repo, Docker image, Kubernetes Deployment and autoscaler, plus its own SLOs and response shapes. Inside ShopMobileEdge, CheckoutIntake handlers validate mobile checkout submissions and CheckoutReserve workers call InventoryService over a 200-connection limit to reserve stock. During sneaker drops intake peaks near 12000 submissions per minute while InventoryService sustains about 900 reservations per minute at 250 ms p95. Intake and reservation are wired inline today, so handlers block on the slower downstream, retries pile up, pod RSS exceeds its 4 GB limit and pods get OOMKilled, while in quiet periods reservation capacity sits idle and handler threads wait. Mobile clients require explicit overload signals with 429 plus Retry-After instead of silent loss, accepted reservations must not be lost, and intake must stay responsive during bursts.

rationale: native Android and iOS apps reach only ShopMobileEdge while the browser app reaches only ShopWebEdge, two independently deployable gateways aggregating the same downstream services differently

state: MedTrace tracks pharmaceutical packs across manufacturers, distributors, pharmacies and a regulator. Nine independent organizations each operate a ReplicaNode in its own data center. Each node keeps a full copy of pack registrations and handoffs as hash-chained append-only records and runs deterministic validation code. A batch of updates becomes settled only after more than two thirds of nodes sign votes for it in numbered rounds with a rotating proposer; edge clients treat a transfer as final only after seeing that quorum certificate. Edge clients FactoryEdgeApp on packaging lines, PharmacyTill in stores and CustomsScanner at borders never contact nodes directly. They send proposals through IngressGateway into a shared SubmitQueue over AMQP, and all execution outcomes plus settlement proofs return through one shared ResultQueue to limit connections. A single site may have 400 proposals in flight, results arrive out of order minutes later after voting rounds complete, some proposals are rejected for duplicate serials, and retries must not cause double apply. Gateway, nodes and edge apps are owned by different teams with no shared domain objects, and new client types are added yearly without changing existing clients.

state: FairGoods runs a provenance network where four retailer and three certifier organizations each operate a peer node holding a tamper-evident append-only log of asset transfers. Client submissions go to an Endorser pool that simulates contract logic and collects endorsements, then to an Ordering cluster that sequences transactions into batches; each peer validates batches via quorum voting and appends them to its local copy, so all copies converge without a central database. The public Explorer portal has PortalGateway, ProvenanceQuery service and ExplorerUI renderer: PortalGateway routes shopper and auditor requests to ProvenanceQuery, which reads the local peer copy and hands a model to ExplorerUI for HTML output. Each asset page shows a site shell (header, navigation, certifier banner, footer) plus asset timeline, current custody proof, vote summary and certifier comments. Today ExplorerUI builds each asset page by copying shell markup and row markup into every server page file, so a banner change needs edits in 40 files and custody and comments teams cannot release independently. Recall spikes demand per-region output reuse and per-section access rules for embargoed comments.

label: blockchain-based
rationale: four retailers and three certifiers each operate a peer holding a tamper-evident append-only log, with endorsements collected before an ordering cluster sequences batches and peers validate them by quorum

state: PharmaTrack tracks custody of temperature-controlled lots across four orgs (two makers, a carrier, a regulator). Each org runs three ValidatorPeers in its own data center (12 peers total) plus an OrderingCluster of five sequencers in separate regions. A deterministic CustodyProgram runs redundantly on every ValidatorPeer: a transfer proposal from ShipperApp must collect matching execution results from at least eight peers, then the OrderingCluster assigns it a global sequence number, then each peer appends a hash-linked entry binding payload hash, prev hash and sequencer signature and applies the update to its local copy. No central DB is authoritative; a diverged peer is ignored until it replays. ExplorerService in the regulator org indexes confirmed entries into Postgres and serves them to AuditClient browsers and NightlySync jobs over HTTPS JSON as GET /custody-events?lot=...&offset=...&limit=.... The collection grows by 40k entries per day to tens of millions, ordered by sequence number. Deep offset queries scan and sort, time out past 500k rows, and concurrent appends during scrolling shift positions so UI infinite scroll shows duplicates and NightlySync misses rows. Responses must stay under 200KB, remain stateless HTTP with no DB cursor held across requests, and support both human scroll and exact full-history export. Peers talk gRPC with mutual TLS.

state: ShopFast grocery checkout splits update handling and display handling into separate deployables with separate stores. CheckoutWriter (Python FastAPI, 3 replicas) owns all changes: POST /carts/{id}/lines, DELETE /carts/{id}/lines/{lineId} and POST /carts/{id}/submit. It loads a Cart with its Lines from WriterDb (Postgres normalized tables carts, cart_lines, shoppers with credit_limit) into behavior-rich Python classes, checks that cart total stays within the shopper credit limit and that no line quantity drops below zero, saves the whole Cart plus Lines in one Postgres transaction, then appends an immutable past-tense record to FactsLog (Kafka topic shopfast.facts). A Projector worker consumes FactsLog and builds flat denormalized docs in ReaderDb (OpenSearch index order_history plus Redis cache for catalog listings). HistoryReader (Python FastAPI, 8 replicas, p95 under 80ms at 20k rpm) serves GET /history and GET /search only from ReaderDb and never touches WriterDb; CheckoutWriter never serves listings. Shopper data is referenced from carts only by shopper_id, never by embedding. Concurrent browsers may add lines to the same cart while a submit is in flight, and projector lag must stay under 2s.

state: TicketForge sells reserved seating for venues. SubmissionGateway accepts ReserveHold, ConfirmHold and ReleaseHold intents and applies them to HoldLedger, a normalized transactional store that is the sole authority for inventory changes. ProjectorWorker subscribes to committed ledger entries and maintains SeatMapViews and OrderHistoryViews inside ViewTables, a denormalized document store tuned for fast browsing under flash-sale load. BrowseGateway serves SeatAvailability, VenueCalendar and OrderHistory reads exclusively from ViewTables and never touches HoldLedger. SubmissionGateway with HoldLedger and BrowseGateway with ViewTables build, deploy and scale independently, bridged only by ProjectorWorker with at-least-once idempotent upserts. The Hold cluster owns startUtc, expiryUtc, status and price lines. Team practice says expiryUtc must be after startUtc, status may only move HELD to CONFIRMED or HELD to RELEASED, and quotedTotal must equal the sum of line amounts, yet constructors and mutators check nothing and the rules live only in wiki pages. Last month an expiryUtc before startUtc and a backward CONFIRMED to HELD move were stored, then copied faithfully into SeatMapViews, freezing 400 seats as unavailable until manual repair. The team wants invalid creates and transitions to fail immediately at the Hold boundary even when views are stale or the projector lags.

state: NorthStar Telecom runs ContractCenter with two isolated paths and stores. The SubmissionGateway accepts amendment forms from agents, validates business rules, appends to LedgerDB (normalized Postgres) and emits AmendmentAccepted events to Kafka. A separate ViewBuilder consumes those events and maintains SnapshotStore (denormalized Cassandra) with prejoined customer, pricing and discount data for the portal. The PortalLookupAPI and BillingEngine never touch LedgerDB; they serve all customer and invoice lookups from SnapshotStore, which scales independently during month-end billing spikes. Each corporate contract has a stable contractNumber but about 40 attributes that move together: monthly fee, data cap, overage rates, discounts, contact address and signatories. Today LedgerDB keeps one mutable row per contractNumber with lastModifiedAt, so a backdated correction overwrites what billing saw last month, disputes about what terms applied on 1 March are unanswerable, and reproducing an invoice requires digging through Kafka logs. Auditors require answering what the full contract stated on any past date and keeping later amendments from altering references held by open disputes. The team needs a representation inside both LedgerDB and SnapshotStore that preserves identity across amendments while keeping every past full state retrievable for portal history and for BillingEngine repricing.

state: Northwind Retail has three squads each running its own AWS account with Postgres, S3 bucket and Flink job. Team Atlas runs Checkout Ledger ingest, Team Beacon runs Fraud Signals aggregates, Team Cartwheel runs Delivery Routes store. Each squad publishes Parquet shares with schema, retention and SLO docs into a Shared Catalog Index and serves reads directly from its bucket via a Trino gateway; there is no central warehouse team or shared ETL. The Catalog Index backing store is a Registry DB with a SchemaEntry table plus LineageEdge and StewardAudit tables. During launch week Atlas and Beacon stewards open the same SchemaEntry row for checkout_events v14 in browsers, edit columns and retention over several minutes, then PUT. Last month one PUT silently erased a PII flag set by the other, with no error, and Beacon's filter broke. The service keeps one short transaction per read and one per write, holds no locks while users think, and must keep PUT latency under 200ms with an audit trail of rejected saves.

state: RetailCo runs Checkout, Inventory and Risk as autonomous squads. Each squad operates its own Postgres, its own versioned S3 prefix of Parquet extracts with SLO docs and schema entry in the Shared Registry, and its own read API; there is no central warehouse team. Risk and Finance join Checkout history by subscribing to the Checkout prefix through the Policy Gateway, which checks access contracts and emits lineage to the Discovery Portal. Inside Checkout, the Keeper API, the Bulk Import Job and the Address Correction Worker all manage shipment plans: one header row in shipment_plan, child rows in plan_stop and stop_parcel, plus customs rows in stop_form. Today each caller opens a transaction, inserts the header to get its key, loops to insert stops, parcels and forms in FK order, then issues deletes for rows missing from the edit. Missed deletes leave orphan stops, partial failures strand parcels, and any column rename breaks three callers. Stops, parcels and forms are never queried alone, never referenced by Inventory or Risk, and have no meaning without their plan; edits always arrive as a full edited plan from the UI form that must be stored or removed atomically.

state: FreshMart runs 180 supermarkets. Each shop houses a Store Cabinet Server, a rack unit in the back room connected by LAN to POS Terminals, Self Checkouts, Electronic Shelf Labels and a Receipt Printer Service. The cabinet keeps a local copy of catalogue entries for items stocked in that shop and authorizes sales, applies promotions and reprints receipts while the WAN link is down, often for days during storms. A Central Catalogue Service in the company data center owns master product data, national price updates and tax tables. A Nightly Sync Job ships deltas to all cabinets when links are up, and a Price Feed Importer inside each cabinet applies them to local storage. A Product has stable fields such as barcode, name and category plus two fields that change often: shelfPrice and vatRate, updated for seasons, supplier costs and tax law. Auditors and return desks must reproduce what a customer paid on a prior date using only the cabinet during outages. Today the cabinet overwrites shelfPrice and vatRate on each import and keeps a separate PriceHistory table. Every caller -- POS logic, returns, audit reports -- hand-writes date comparisons against that table, with off-by-one day mistakes causing reprinted totals to differ from originals and month-end reports to disagree.

state: VineSight manages irrigation and disease response for 42 vineyards. Each vineyard has a shed cabinet holding a VineyardHub computer wired directly to its ProbeArray soil probes, CanopyCam cameras and ValveBank irrigation valves. The VineyardHub runs MildewDetector on images and IrrigationPlanner for watering schedules on site, so spray and valve commands issue within seconds even when the cellular link to VineSightCloud is down for hours. VineSightCloud only receives nightly summaries, ships model weights south, and hosts Dashboard for agronomists. All vineyard, probe, valve and batch identifiers are 36-character strings and all times are plain integers: valve pulse lengths in milliseconds, probe polling periods in seconds, blackout windows in minutes. Last month a test harness passed a probe id where a valve id was expected and flooded two rows, and a planner patch passed a polling period where a pulse length was expected and overwatered by 1000x. Functions like schedule_open(valve, vineyard, probe, duration) and log_sample(vineyard, probe, batch) take several same-shaped arguments and reviews keep missing swaps. Shed computers run on limited power with no operator, so mistakes must be caught before shipment rather than by extra runtime checks that get skipped under load.

state: GreenWave Corridor manages 42 signalized junctions for a mid-size city. Each junction has a roadside cabinet that houses a CabinetProcessor, a SensorFusion unit, a PhaseScheduler and a SlotBookkeeper, plus a SignalHeadDriver that drives the lamps. Cameras, induction loops, pedestrian buttons and short-range bus radios feed SensorFusion over the cabinet LAN; PhaseScheduler issues lamp commands to SignalHeadDriver within 40 ms of detection. A city data center hosts the CorridorHub which builds nightly timing plans from counts and pushes them to cabinets; a DriverApp in vehicles receives wait estimates by direct radio from the local CabinetProcessor. Cabinets must run alone up to 72 hours when fiber is cut, journaling counts and deviations for later upload, and tolerate clocks drifting 2 seconds from the hub. The hard local rules are: two conflicting movements must never show green together, minimum green plus clearance times from the city safety table must always hold, and a bus or fire-truck crossing slot must never be given to two claimants for overlapping seconds. Vehicle detections, pedestrian calls and priority requests arrive at the same time from different inputs, and a nightly plan can arrive while an override is active. Today lamp states and bookings live in separate files updated by different code paths, so a crash between writes can leave a green that overlaps a booked crossing.

state: NorthStar Mutual runs PolicyAdmin on a COBOL mainframe with MQ, WebClaimIntake on Java Spring with HTTPS, RiskScoring on Python with gRPC, LedgerPosting on SAP with RFC, and CustomerNotify on a SaaS email API. No application calls another directly. Every request is sent to TransitHub, a separately deployed cluster that validates, routes, translates schemas between COBOL copybooks, JSON and IDocs, and bridges MQ, HTTPS, gRPC and RFC via per-system adapters such as MainframeAdapter and SapAdapter. WebClaimIntake containers are memory-capped and legally barred from bundling the SAP SDK and mainframe client libs at 450MB licensed per host. LedgerPosting releases monthly while WebClaimIntake releases daily. Today the shared operation definitions for fileClaim, postLedgerEntry and scoreRisk live inside the adapter packages, so building WebClaimIntake drags in MQ headers, SAP jars and copybook parsers, breaking builds and violating license rules. The architects must decide where to keep those shared operation definitions and how clients obtain references to backend capabilities without packaging the adapter implementations.

state: Meridian Freight runs three incompatible line-of-business endpoints: OrderCapture exposes SOAP/XML on WebSphere, StockLedger exposes REST/JSON in Python, and FreightPartner drops EDI flat files over SFTP. None calls another directly. Every inbound document is picked up by protocol adapters SoapIntake, RestIntake and FileIntake and forwarded as a canonical envelope to CentralFlow, a centrally operated mediation tier that validates, transforms, routes and delivers to the correct downstream endpoint. Inside CentralFlow a pool of eight ValidationWorkers blocks on an in-memory work queue fed by the adapters. On Kubernetes rolling updates CentralFlow receives SIGTERM with 30 seconds grace: adapters must stop accepting new files and requests immediately, yet 2000-5000 envelopes already queued must still be validated and routed before the pod exits. The queue API offers blocking take with no native end-of-stream marker. Killing threads mid-work loses customer orders and leaves partial audit writes; leaving threads blocked keeps the pod in Terminating and blocks the rollout. The team needs an orderly shutdown approach that works with only the existing queue.

state: Northwind Retail operates OrderPipeline with a single shared ExchangeHub deployed as a clustered process in its private network. Three surrounding systems use incompatible protocols and payloads: SapLedger speaks RFC with IDoc documents, SalesCloud speaks HTTPS REST with JSON, and StockDB speaks TCP SQL with XML extracts. None of them call each other directly. Every exchange is sent to the hub, where InboundGateway normalizes the envelope, RoutingCore applies content rules, TransformationEngine converts IDoc/JSON/XML to a canonical Order record, and OutboundGateway delivers to the destination through a plug-in adapter. Each adapter currently needs three collaborating objects to work: a Connection that holds credentials and session, a Sender that issues remote calls, and a Converter that maps between the canonical record and the vendor format. OrderFlow code directly instantiates SapConnection with SapSender and SapConverter in six places keyed on strings like sap and crm. Adding StockDB required edits in all six places, and a recent incident paired a SalesCloud connection with a Sap converter, failing only during settlement. The team wants one startup wiring point keyed by vendor name that hands out the three objects that belong to the same vendor together, so fulfillment logic never mentions concrete classes and a new vendor is added by registering one entry.

state: Acme Packaging runs order usage accounting across two estates. In its Detroit plant computer room, two rack-mounted systems emit the same production usage facts: LineHistorians (Siemens WinCC on Windows servers) drop fixed-width shift files with imperial counts and MM/DD/YYYY timestamps to an SFTP drop, and LabLIMS pushes nightly CSV exports with metric counts, ISO dates, and extra lab notes columns. A third source, a 3PL partner, posts spreadsheet XML exports to an S3 bucket in AWS us-east-1, using partner SKUs, euro pallets, and free-text remarks. All three land at UsageIntake, a service on EKS in us-east-1 connected to the plant via Direct Connect with mTLS, which must hand records to RatingEngine and LedgerPoster (also on EKS) for rating and ledger posting. RatingEngine today branches on source id with nested ifs for field names, units, currencies, and date parsing, and each partner onboarding copies that branching. Producers cannot be changed: WinCC formats are frozen, LIMS upgrades on its own cycle, partner layouts vary by contract. UsageIntake must absorb per-source layout knowledge so downstream logic sees exactly one record shape with validated units and dates, while adding a new partner only touches per-format code.

state: Meridian Auto Parts runs PlantScan Ingest on rack servers in the basement of its Detroit factory building, writing every pallet move to PlantStore, a Postgres instance on the next rack for sub-millisecond scanner ack. CentralCatalog, a catalog and ordering service, runs in a provider-managed Kubernetes cluster in eu-central-1 billed per pod-second and backed by CatalogDB. The two sites are linked only by an 80 ms site-to-site VPN tunnel with nightly maintenance windows. A Nightly Reconciler job runs in the eu-central-1 cluster: it pulls the day's PlantStore deltas over the tunnel, re-reads CatalogDB rows by SKU and by pallet membership join, applies quantity corrections, and pushes adjustments back to PlantStore. With 42000 SKUs and 180000 pallet links the job re-reads the same PartRow many times through different queries. Engineers see divergent in-memory copies: the SKU path and the pallet path each build a separate Part object for part 4521-B, quantity edits on one copy are invisible to the other, the later database write silently overwrites the earlier, and each repeat load pays another VPN round trip. The team must choose a session-level load strategy for the Reconciler run that reuses already loaded Part objects, collapses repeat reads, and makes all services in the run observe identical field values.

state: Northwind Tools keeps its PartsStock PostgreSQL 15 cluster inside its company-operated data center in Frankfurt for export-control compliance; tables parts_stock(part_no, bin_no, qty, lot_code) and suppliers cannot leave that site. ReceivingDesk intake service and PickingController run as VMs on that same site network and read and write those tables directly. Customer-facing StorefrontAPI (AWS Lambda plus API Gateway in eu-central-1), nightly ReplenishmentForecaster (ECS scheduled job) and ReturnsPortal backend all reach the Frankfurt cluster over a private Direct Connect link through PgBouncer in the DMZ, with a read replica on RDS in eu-central-1 for dashboards. Each team pasted SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE text for parts_stock into its own codebase with different placeholder styles, column orders and timeout handling. Adding lot_code and retiring bin_no broke StorefrontAPI and Forecaster in ways no review could predict, DBAs cannot find all statements to tune or audit, and every caller must know driver details and type mapping. The teams share a versioned Python package between both sites and need schema changes and tuning to touch a single reviewable place, with rows passed to screens and jobs as plain dicts and lists and no behavior-rich domain layer, since a full mapper would add more machinery than it removes for these few tables.

label: hybrid-cloud
rationale: the parts-stock cluster stays in a company-operated data centre for export-control reasons while the customer-facing storefront runs on managed cloud functions and a managed gateway

state: CityFlow tracks downtown bus delays. EdgeIngest validates GPS pings (12k per sec peak) and appends them to DurableLog, an ordered durable topic with 90-day retention that is the only source of truth. FlowEngine is a long-running Python job on six 8GB workers that reads DurableLog in order, fetches zone fare rules for each ping from ZoneDB (Postgres), computes five-minute delay aggregates, and upserts results into ServeDB (ScyllaDB) read by TripAPI. AdminConsole edits ZoneDB a few times per week; the top 40 zone ids cover 92 percent of pings. When operators correct fare rules or fix aggregation code, ReplayManager clears ServeDB and restarts the same FlowEngine binary from offset zero to rebuild state through identical code; there is no second offline computation path. A recent rebuild from zero saturated ZoneDB at its 200-connection ceiling, p95 per-event handling rose to 480 ms, rebuild lag reached 14 hours, and live pings queued behind the backlog. Ops require an edit to affect TripAPI within five minutes; longer stale fares cause billing disputes.

label: kappa-architecture
rationale: an ordered durable log with 90-day retention is the only source of truth and one long-running job is the only computation over it, so a rebuild replays the same log instead of a separate offline path

state: CityFlow at NorthStar Mobility handles trip fares and driver payouts. RiderApp and DriverApp send trip, fare and card-token events to TripIngress, which validates and appends them to OrderedLog, a retained ordered topic holding every raw event for 400 days. FlowProcessor is the only computation over that history: a Flink job that reads OrderedLog from the latest offset for live updates to PayoutLiveTable behind LiveOpsBoard, and when thresholds change ReplayManager restarts the same Flink job from offset zero to rebuild PayoutLiveTable and MonthlySettlementView without any separate nightly job or warehouse export. AdminConsole lets ops staff issue payout blocks, manual fare corrections and threshold edits that go through AccountService and also land in OrderedLog. Compliance requires proof for PCI DSS and state audits that each privileged adjustment and each access to full card numbers is attributable and unchanged months later. Today AccountService writes local files that the same service account can overwrite, rotate or truncate, missing entries leave no trace, and denied override attempts are often not written at all. Card tokens are expanded to full PAN inside FlowProcessor for fraud checks, so those values appear in debug dumps and in the local files.

label: kappa-architecture
rationale: a retained ordered topic holds every raw event for 400 days and a single streaming job is the only computation over that history, serving both live views and replays

state: MarketPulse scores payment events for fraud. EdgeIngestor validates PaymentEvents and appends them to EventLog, an immutable durable ordered store retained for 90 days. DetectionEngine is a long-lived Python job that reads EventLog from the latest offset, maintains rolling RiskTables in RocksDB, and exposes them through QueryAPI for dashboards and blocking checks. When scoring logic changes, ReplayCoordinator restarts the same DetectionEngine binary from offset zero over the retained EventLog to rebuild RiskTables, with live traffic continuing to append during the rebuild; there is no separate offline cluster. DetectionEngine hosts partner-supplied Detector modules in-process for custom rules. For each 5-second tumbling window, Scheduler hands a Detector a direct reference to a TenantLedger object (methods getBalance, holdFunds, releaseHold) scoped to that tenant and window. Requirement: after the window closes, after tenant unsubscribe, or on policy breach, later calls using the retained reference must fail, while TenantLedger itself stays alive for other windows and tenants. Detectors are untrusted and will not cooperate by dropping references. Audit demands a separate control held only by Scheduler to cut off past grants instantly without tracking down every copy.

label: kappa-architecture
rationale: ingestion appends to an immutable durable ordered store and one long-lived engine reads it from the latest offset while a replay coordinator restarts that same job to recompute

state: CityRide runs DriverPulse, a driver analytics and payout platform ingesting 40M trip events per day. Event Intake (Python FastAPI) appends immutable JSON trip records to LogBus (Kafka), the system of record. Each night Full History Rebuilders (Spark on HDFS) rescan LogBus from day zero and rewrite canonical driver aggregates for earnings, safety counts and payout status into HistoryStore (Cassandra). In parallel Live Delta Engine (Flink on Kubernetes) tails the same LogBus and upserts only the last six hours of changes into HotStore (Redis) within seconds. Merge Gateway (Python GraphQL) answers dashboard and ops UI reads by fetching the same driver id from both HistoryStore and HotStore and combining the two records per request, so results reflect long-term correctness plus seconds-old activity, and rebuild output can overwrite drift in HotStore. The pain is in three Python services - PayoutService, VerificationService, DispatchService - plus two cron jobs, all hitting both stores directly. Each re-derives its own CQL and Redis scans for the same ideas: drivers with overdue payouts, drivers pending verification, drivers with open safety flags. Table names, column families and key encodings leak into fare and eligibility rules, copies drift apart on voided-trip handling, and every domain unit test needs live Cassandra and Redis containers and takes minutes.

label: lambda-architecture
rationale: nightly full-history rebuilders rescan the log from day zero into canonical aggregates while a parallel live job maintains deltas, so batch and speed paths serve the same platform

state: PaySight processes card transactions for 400 stores. EdgeIngest validates POS events and appends them to Kafka topic tx-events and to an append-only HDFS archive. NightlyRecompute is a Spark job on a YARN cluster that rereads the whole archive from day zero and overwrites the FullTotals table in Cassandra with per-merchant daily sums and risk flags. LiveIncrement is a Flink deployment that consumes tx-events and upserts per-minute deltas into the RecentDeltas table in the same Cassandra ring. MergeServe is a stateless query tier that on each dashboard read fetches one row from FullTotals and the matching rows from RecentDeltas and adds them together before returning. ReferenceStore is a Postgres database holding MerchantMaster rows plus dependent addresses and settlement accounts; its snapshot is broadcast to both NightlyRecompute and LiveIncrement for joins. AnalystWorkbench is a web app where risk officers open a merchant file, review 90 days of merged history, adjust status, limits and addresses over 10-20 minutes across several saves, then submit. About 30 officers curate 200 merchants per day, so simultaneous edits to the same merchant are uncommon but possible during fraud waves. Holding a Postgres row lock for the whole think time is banned: it would exhaust connections, block the nightly broadcast extract, and stall other officers. A second submit silently overwriting the first has already caused misrouted settlements.

label: lambda-architecture
rationale: a nightly job rereads the whole archive from day zero and overwrites the totals table while a streaming deployment upserts per-minute increments over the same events

state: StreamLens tracks views across 40M daily play events. Play events enter through Edge Ingest Gateway and are appended to Immutable Event Archive (Kafka with S3 backup, never updated in place). Two compute paths derive counts: Nightly Rebuild Cluster (Spark on Kubernetes) scans the full archive each night to recompute authoritative per-video per-collection totals, writing Parquet snapshots to History Store (S3 plus Postgres warehouse). Live Increment Engine (Flink) consumes the same Kafka topic and maintains per-minute deltas for the current day in Hot Counts Cache (Redis), expiring entries after 36h once the nightly job has covered them. Fusion Query API serves GET /stats by adding the last snapshot total to any newer deltas, so dashboards show long-term history plus seconds-old activity. Separately, Catalog Keeper (Python/Django plus Postgres 15) owns editorial metadata: Videos (12M rows) and Curated Collections (80k rows). A video may appear in many collections and a collection holds many videos; both sides browse the relation, curators add or remove memberships from either end, and nightly jobs join membership to events to roll up collection totals. The team debates where to keep membership: adding a collection reference to Videos fails when a video is in five collections, adding a video reference to Collections repeats the problem in reverse, and storing ID lists as text breaks integrity when videos or collections are deleted.

label: lambda-architecture
rationale: a nightly rebuild cluster scans the full immutable archive to recompute authoritative totals while a live path derives increments, and both land in the serving store

state: MercantileSuite handles online orders for a regional grocer. The code base is split into Checkout, Stock, Loyalty and Messaging areas, each owning its tables, jobs and public facade; code in one area may only call the facade of another, never its internals, enforced by package rules and code review. Everything compiles to one runnable service artifact version 3.4 that runs in one JVM per host behind a load balancer; a release restarts all areas together and there are no separate network hops between Checkout and Stock, only direct method invocation with a shared worker fleet and a shared outbound HTTP connection set. Checkout calls Taxlyr external pricing API and a card processor, Messaging calls an external mail vendor that has recently become slow, sometimes taking 20 seconds to answer. During a vendor slowdown all request threads pile up waiting for mail responses, Stock lookups from store staff and new checkouts queue behind mail waits and then drop, even though they never use mail. Ops wants Checkout, Stock queries and Messaging sends to keep working independently when one external peer stalls, without adding new deployables.

state: FreshCart runs its grocery backend as one Python service image launched as one OS process. Code is divided into Ordering, Stock and Fulfillment slices. Each slice owns its tables in the same Postgres database and its own Python packages. Cross-slice access is allowed only through explicit public functions; Ordering never touches Fulfillment tables directly. Requests flow from the FastAPI handlers in Ordering into Stock.reserve() then into Fulfillment.PickQueue.add(job). A fixed pool of 12 picker threads in Fulfillment calls PickQueue.take() to get jobs for packing stations. Peak bursts reach 2000 jobs in minutes, queue capacity is capped at 500 to bound memory. Today take() returns None when empty and add() raises QueueFull when full. Picker threads loop with sleep(0.05) retrying take(), and Ordering handlers retry add() with backoff. Under load this burns CPU, adds 200ms p99 latency, and during holiday spikes retries exhaust handler threads and drop checkouts. Product requires no job may be discarded and handler threads must not spin. The team debates how PickQueue should behave when callers arrive while it is empty or full, given that readiness depends on the opposite side making progress at an unknown time.

state: ParcelPilot is built and released as one executable jar run on a Kubernetes Deployment with a single Postgres instance where each business area owns its tables. Code is split into strictly isolated packages: ScanIntake exposes REST ingestion, RoutePlanner computes sortation paths, BillingSettlement invoices shippers, AuditTrail keeps compliance records. Cross-area access is allowed only through public interfaces and an in-process event bus; direct table reads and ad-hoc static calls fail ArchUnit checks. At peak sortation ScanIntake accepts up to 18000 scan events per sec with a 200ms HTTP SLO, while RoutePlanner sustains only 4000 plans per sec due to graph search at 80 to 250ms per event. Today Intake invokes Planner inline, so bursts exhaust request threads, heap exceeds 3GB, and a slow plan delays scanner acknowledgment. Operations requires heap under 2GB, no silent loss, and scanners receive a fast 202 with tracking id while planning proceeds in background. The team needs a handoff where intake and planning advance at their own paces, bursts are absorbed up to a fixed limit, and exceeding that limit triggers an explicit policy such as reject with retry-after or spill to durable storage instead of unbounded growth.

state: HarborShare runs voyage capacity planning for container ships. US planners use PlannerWeb-US served from AWS Amplify in us-east-1 backed by SessionAPI on AWS EKS; EU planners use PlannerWeb-EU served from Azure Static Web Apps in West Europe backed by AllocAPI on Azure AKS. Both APIs read and write the same VoyageLedger stored in AWS RDS Postgres in us-east-1 with an async replica exposed via Azure Database for PostgreSQL in West Europe, linked by a private interconnect with 80-120ms round trip and a cross-provider event bus (AWS EventBridge forwarded to Azure Service Bus) for invalidation. A planning session for voyage VY-440 lasts 20-40 minutes: the planner loads slot totals, customer holds and weight limits, then issues 10-25 separate save calls while negotiating by phone. During peak season two planners often open the same voyage to promise the same scarce reefer slots to different customers. Database transactions cannot stay open across think time due to timeouts and connection limits, and late rejection discards half an hour of negotiation. Product requires that once a planner starts work, conflicting edits are blocked rather than merged later, with automatic expiry after 45 minutes and an override queue for supervisors.

state: GlobalSure operates a travel-claim platform with execution split across vendors. ClaimIngress runs on AWS Lambda in us-east-1 and validates incoming filings, ClaimScoring runs on Azure Functions in West Europe and applies fraud and pricing rules, and SettlementSupervisor runs on AWS Fargate in us-east-1 to schedule payouts. All three share one logical operational store: primary tables live in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL in us-east-1, asynchronously replicated to a read replica on Azure Database for PostgreSQL in West Europe for low-latency reads by the scoring path. Product rules require identical selections everywhere: overdue document requests, pending medical reviews, and open high-value cases. Today each service hand-writes its own SQLAlchemy Core fragments and raw SQL for those selections, embedding table and column names directly in adjudication logic. The copies have drifted, a recent column rename broke scoring but not ingress, and unit tests for pricing rules now need a live database container with seeded fixtures. Release policy demands that schema edits stay isolated to persistence code, that duplicate selection logic converge to a single maintained definition, and that domain rules be verifiable with fast in-process fakes.

state: StreamVault operates a film catalog with write and read paths placed on different vendors. IngestAPI runs on EKS in AWS us-east-1 and accepts curator edits to Films and Performers, validating input and writing to CatalogPrimary. CuratorPortal runs on AKS in Azure West Europe and serves browse queries for Films by Performer and Performers by Film. CatalogPrimary is a Postgres database in AWS us-east-1; CatalogReplica is a Postgres read replica in Azure West Europe. SyncBridge is a Kafka-based change feed that ships row changes from the primary to the replica with at-least-once delivery and idempotent apply, so reads in Azure observe writes from AWS within seconds. Domain rule: a Film lists many Performers and a Performer appears in many Films, with collections navigable from both ends in Python domain objects. The pairing itself carries no extra attributes; pay and billing details live in other records. Constraints: concurrent curators through IngestAPI must not create duplicate Film-Performer pairs; deleting a Film or Performer must remove its pairings without leaving orphans; listings must be retrievable efficiently from either end under heavy read load on the replica; writes use serializable transactions on the primary with sub-100ms p95 for single-film fetch.

state: Field ops runs a fleet console for 40 survey drones built as a tree of self-contained interactive units. The root FleetHub has three collaborators: HubView renders maps and alerts, HubStore keeps fleet state and mission rules, HubLiaison keeps the two in sync and alone talks to other units. Each drone gets a child DroneCard with the same split: CardView shows telemetry and risk, CardStore holds track, battery and plan, CardLiaison mediates between its view and store and exchanges updates only with the parent HubLiaison and through it with sibling cards. No view contacts a store directly and no store talks across units. Hub runs on the ops server, cards run on field tablets and are created on takeoff and removed on landing, each listening on a temporary NATS subject. For risk scoring each CardLiaison sends a JSON task packet to a shared ScoringService in Go that owns the thermal model. The service cannot dial tablets directly behind NAT with changing IPs and must not keep a registry of cards. Operators need each score to surface in the originating card view within 4 seconds even with 30 concurrent asks.

state: AeroGate manages tower surface traffic from two deployment sites. The equipment-room server hosts shared holdings and top coordination while each tower console hosts workspace panes for runways, strips and weather. Every pane is built as a closed trio: RunwayPresentation with RunwayAbstraction and RunwayControl, StripPresentation with StripAbstraction and StripControl, WeatherPresentation with WeatherAbstraction and WeatherControl. Inside a trio the visual part exchanges events only with its control part, the control part reads and writes its abstraction part and negotiates upward with the top coordination, and the abstraction part never calls the visual part directly. StripAbstraction internally models FlightPlan, TaxiSegment and Clearance as small interlinked objects with dozens of getters used freely by server-side scheduling logic. Console refresh currently invokes those getters over authenticated RPC field by field: one StripPresentation paint triggers 40 to 60 round trips with TLS and authorization on each call and paint time above 800 ms against a 250 ms budget at 30 consoles. Direct serialization of the graph fails on cycles and lazy ORM proxies and would expose internals. The team must keep the fine-grained interfaces for local scheduling while letting a console complete a full strip refresh in one round trip with a boundary type that holds no business rules.

state: PortOps Harbor Console is a Python 3.11 server-rendered operations board for a container terminal, deployed on two replicated app servers backed by Postgres with thin browsers that receive finished HTML and post forms back. It is built as a hierarchy of UI units. The top HarborOverview unit owns three cooperating parts: OverviewRender for HTML and input events, OverviewStore for vessels, berths and tide records, and OverviewBroker that keeps the two consistent and talks to other units. Middle units BerthPlan and TrafficMap repeat the triple as BerthRender/BerthStore/BerthBroker and TrafficRender/TrafficStore/TrafficBroker. Leaf units TugRoster and GateQueue repeat it as TugRender/TugStore/TugBroker and GateRender/GateStore/GateBroker. Inside each unit Render never touches the database and Store never emits markup; all cross-unit traffic goes Broker to Broker up and down the tree. The current pain is page assembly. HarborOverview, BerthPlan, TrafficMap and three nightly reports each embed copies of the harbor header, tide banner, side navigation, footer and repeated row markup for tugs and gates. A logo or tariff change means editing nine server functions and three jobs, copies have drifted, the tug team cannot release its roster section without a full page release, and operators need per-role hiding of GateQueue while the tide banner could be reused for five minutes while the rest stays fresh.

state: StreamPulse processes live device telemetry for 40 tenants. EdgeIngest validates sensor frames and appends them to StreamHub log partitions keyed by tenant. FlowCoordinator routes ordered batches to a pool of DetectorRunner pods that host third-party detection modules in a sandboxed Python runtime. Each module runs on a single-threaded event loop and never blocks: it consumes a batch, emits derived alerts to AlertFold, and signals how many further batches it can accept; upstream stages pause when downstream queues fill and resume when space frees, keeping p99 latency under 300ms during 10x spikes. DetectorRunner scales independently from EdgeIngest. For each job, JobSupervisor lends the module a TenantWindow handle that reads and checkpoints that tenant's rolling state in SharedStateStore. Modules often stash the handle in closures and keep timers alive after the job. On job completion, tenant logout, or a policy breach detected by PolicyWatch, SharedStateStore must stay alive for other jobs but that module's future calls must fail immediately, without its cooperation and via a control held only by JobSupervisor. Latency budget forbids extra auth checks on the hot path beyond one indirection.

label: reactive-architecture
rationale: routing feeds single-threaded event loops that never block, emitting derived alerts downstream while consumers advertise demand and producers stall when buffers fill

state: Live odds distribution platform turns exchange ticks into subscriber feeds. TickerIngress normalizes venue updates and pushes them into bounded non-blocking queues feeding a pool of PriceRefiner workers, each pinned to its own event loop. PriceRefiner stages enrich, validate and join ticks, then forward results toward EdgeFanout which holds per-connection queues for thousands of sockets. Downstream stages return demand credits upstream; when a queue fills the producer pauses instead of blocking threads, and autoscaled refiner replicas absorb bursts. LedgerArchiver persists settled batches off the hot path via a separate sink channel. Core types are C++: PositionBatch holds a public creation path because the stream runtime must create it through std::make_unique inside generic operator code, yet only BatchAssembler is allowed to create settlement-ready batches. Opening the constructor to all callers lets any operator forge sequence numbers and corrupt ordering relied on by EdgeFanout. Declaring BatchAssembler as a full friend gives it unrestricted reach to cancel, adjust and reprice internals that must stay closed. The team needs a compile-time enforcement where the constructor remains visible for the generic creation path but remains unusable by ordinary handlers except through the designated assembler, with no runtime check and no widening of the public contract.

state: PayStream runs instant driver payouts across three regions. Named components: EdgeGateway terminates driver and ops HTTP on non-blocking event loops and publishes PayoutRequested events; PayoutFlow is a topology of stateless stages that fan out to RiskScorer and LedgerWriter through bounded event channels where each consumer advertises demand and producers stall when buffers fill; LedgerWriter appends to Postgres per shard; AdminPortal lets ops staff issue payout overrides, role grants and fee-config changes that publish AdminAction events back into the same topology; ComplianceSink is a separate deployment that subscribes to all security-relevant events and writes them to WORM storage; Verifier is an offline job run by internal audit. Flow: EdgeGateway -> PayoutFlow -> RiskScorer/LedgerWriter, with AdminAction events joined by correlation id for end-to-end tracing, and all stages autoscaled on Kubernetes by consumer lag with no shared transaction across stages. Constraints: ops engineers hold root on the cluster and can edit local JSONL files that today hold the audit trail; files are rotated by the same process that writes them so a deleted file or missing sequence is not noticed; a DB rollback must not erase the attempt record; auditors must prove after the fact that a line is the line written and detect altered, deleted, reordered or truncated entries for PCI DSS and SOX reviews, while card PANs in payloads must not spread into the trail.

state: FleetPulse is a Python telemetry hub tracking 40+ vehicle sensor types. Its deployment is one long-lived service: IngestGateway keeps accepting MQTT traffic while ModelHarvester watches the models directory. When an operator drops a new dataclass file through AdminConsole, ModelHarvester imports the module without restart, reads its type annotations, field defaults and Column tags, and refreshes the central TypeCatalog that lists every loaded class, its fields and target tables in PostgresStore. PersistenceDriver subscribes to TypeCatalog change events and at once rebuilds its insert, update and select routines plus type converters from the fresh entries, so the next reading for a new sensor type is stored with no code edit and no downtime. Classes under models hold only state and validation helpers with no SQL, no save methods and no table strings. Constraints: 3 to 5 new types per week, frequent column renames, Postgres only, and domain tests must run without a database by swapping the store side.

state: Sentinel is a live fraud-screening fabric processing payment events in a Kubernetes cluster without restarts. StreamRouter forwards each event through a chain of Detector containers such as VelocityCheck, DeviceFingerprint and GeoAnomaly. LiveTopologyStore holds an in-memory graph of which Detector instances are running and how StreamRouter connects them. PerformanceSampler scrapes per-detector latency and false-positive rates every 5s and annotates that graph. RewireCoordinator runs a control loop every 30s: it reads LiveTopologyStore plus the annotated metrics, decides to spin up, retire or reorder Detector containers, then writes the new graph back to LiveTopologyStore and pushes updated routes to StreamRouter over gRPC. All changes happen while traffic flows. For durability, BlueprintLibrary on Postgres 15 persists reusable TuningBlueprints and DetectorSpecs. A blueprint declares a set of specs it needs; one spec is reused across dozens of blueprints, for example GeoAnomaly in retail, travel and ATM blueprints. Operators query both directions: list specs for a blueprint to render the editor, and list blueprints using a spec to assess blast radius before retiring a detector. Deletes must not leave orphan pairings, duplicate pairings must be rejected by the store, and all writes go through one admin API to avoid split-brain updates. Pairings carry no extra data.

label: reflection-architecture
rationale: an in-memory graph of which detectors are running and how the router connects them is inspected and rewired through an admin API while the fabric keeps running without restarts

state: CityWorks Permit Hub handles commercial building permits for a metro region. Browser-based PermitWorkspace lets inspectors open a case file with applicant data, drawing references, fee lines and approval notes, edit over 40-90 minutes across many short requests, then file a final save to PermitStore in Postgres. SessionCoordinator tracks open edit sessions and routes each request to current service implementations. Every service FeeCalc, DrawingCheck and NoteEnrich publishes a self-description of its operations and accepted case schema to LiveTypeDirectory. All of them run side by side in one cluster. RewireController watches the directory plus latency and error counters, then hot-swaps service builds and pushes new routing tables to SessionCoordinator without downtime; when a running module changes its directory entry is updated, so the directory and the live deployment stay linked both ways. Two district offices can open the same case P-1187 during storm-repair surges. Each loads the same fee lines and notes, works independently, and the later final save quietly discards the earlier inspector's fee adjustments and conditions. Keeping one database transaction held open across think time, interruptions and closed laptops is barred by operations. Matcher scans FactStore against the active bundle each cycle and emits a ConflictSet of satisfied entries. Selector orders the ConflictSet by salience and recency. Actuator applies the selected entry, updates FactStore and loops until quiescence, then hands PayoutInstruction and ReviewFlag to LedgerWriter and AuditLog. PolicyTable bundles hot-swap without redeploying Matcher/Selector/Actuator. state: AutoUnderwrite processes small-business loan applications. IntakeGateway validates uploads and asserts ApplicantFacts (income, debt, bureau score, sector code) into WorkingMemory, a shared fact store. Analysts author several hundred WHEN <conditions over facts> THEN <assert, retract or update> clauses in ClausePortal; bundles are versioned in ClauseRepository and hot-swapped without a code deploy. At runtime Matcher runs an incremental network over WorkingMemory to find satisfied antecedents, Agenda orders activations by salience and recency, and ConsequenceExecutor fires the selected consequences, updating facts and finally emitting an UnderwritingVerdict to DecisionPublisher and AuditLog. Matcher, Agenda and Executor deploy and scale as separate containers. The pain point is UnderwritingVerdict, now a Python dataclass with a status string plus optional approved_limit, rate, denial_codes, referral_queue and sla_due fields. Two recent incidents left both approved_limit and denial_codes populated, causing Agenda to schedule conflicting follow-ons and auditors to flag ambiguous outcomes. Every consumer re-checks which fields align with status, and a planned ReferredWithConditions outcome next quarter means hunting all status tests across Matcher clauses and Python consumers.

state: NorthStar Lending operates CheckPoint for personal loan approvals. IntakeGateway receives applications and appends applicant facts to FactLedger in Postgres. MatcherWorker polls FactLedger, loads about 240 WHEN/THEN clauses from PolicyRepo, a Git backed store that reloads without restart, evaluates antecedents against facts and pushes matches onto AgendaQueue, a Redis sorted set ordered by salience. ConsequenceRunner pops AgendaQueue, runs THEN actions through NotificationService and LedgerWriter, which may assert derived facts back into FactLedger to trigger further cycles until quiescence. MatcherWorker and ConsequenceRunner deploy as separate Kubernetes deployments that scale independently. Policy authors write clauses in Python using nested calls such as AllOf(AnyOf(GreaterThan(score, 680), LessThan(delinq, 2)), Equals(resident, True)) or sequences of setters on a ConditionBag temporary with names like tmp, t2, aux. Clauses average five conditions. Reviews find swapped numeric thresholds, copy pasted setter blocks where order silently changes meaning, and intent visible only after reading every line. The team wants an underwriting() entry where analysts state credit, residency and delinquency requirements with domain terms in order, without managing temporaries, validated once before registration.

state: TripForge is a single deployable planning service that assembles custom vacation packages by driving bookings across businesses it does not control. Its parts are a Trip Ledger in Postgres, an Outbound Dispatcher, and a single shared Inbound Webhook. External participants are SkyLink Airlines booking API, StayHub hotel inventory API, PaySecure charge API, and RoadWheels car API, each with its own payload shapes and error codes and each exposing hold and cancel or void operations. For a customer itinerary the Planner issues a flight hold, then a hotel hold, then a payment authorization, then a car hold; if the car hold is refused the Planner voids the payment, releases the hotel hold and cancels the flight hold through their respective cancel endpoints, and similar reversal chains apply if another leg fails after retries. At peak the Dispatcher has about 2000 itineraries active, each with up to four outbound attempts in flight, and every provider confirmation, refusal or retry callback arrives on the same inbound webhook and queue. Providers retry callbacks for up to 24 hours and may deliver duplicates out of order. The team cannot create a dedicated callback endpoint per itinerary or per leg, cannot rely on transport ordering, and cannot share a common domain model with providers. It needs a uniform envelope that lets the gateway route on metadata alone while provider payloads travel untouched, plus a way for the Planner to pair each inbound result with the exact outbound attempt that caused it and to drop late duplicates without leaking pending state.

state: AtlasHoliday runs a single managing service called PackManager in Python backed by a PackLedger table in Postgres, fronted by ShopAPI for HTTP checkout, plus a central RabbitMQ broker for async traffic. It sells holiday bundles that combine parties it does not operate: NorthAir for seats, NestStay for rooms, and SafePay for card authorization, each reached over that party's own REST API and reply topics carrier.replies, hotel.replies and pay.replies. For each bundle ShopAPI stores a PENDING row, then PackManager drives the providers one after another: request a seat hold, then a room hold, then a card authorization. Each provider answers minutes to hours later on its topic with accept, decline or timeout. If any stage declines or times out, PackManager reverses earlier successes in opposite order by calling releaseSeat, voidRoomHold and refundAuthorization. Today each provider has a hand-written receive loop in domain code that opens connections, sleeps between polls, parses bytes and acks, duplicating failure handling in three places and tying reaction time to sleep intervals while holding threads idle overnight. The team wants one maintainable receive approach that reacts within seconds of arrival, costs nothing when topics are quiet, and keeps broker client types out of PackLedger logic. Redeploys happen daily and reply bursts can reach 2k per minute at peak.

state: TripCoordinator is a Python deployment run as one container with a Postgres store. It sells bundled trips using parties it does not operate: AirInventory (seat holds over REST), StaySupplier (room holds), PayCore (card charges), RoadCarrier (ground dispatch). Its modules TripPlanner, ChargeHandler and DispatchTracker inside the same process drive a multi-day fulfillment: first request seat holds, then room holds, then charge the card, then dispatch a car, persisting step outcomes in an orders table. Adding a second hotel vendor next quarter would edit planning rules in three places, and unit tests hit the metered PayCore sandbox. IntakeHandler is launched by the cloud vendor only when messages arrive; bursts create hundreds of parallel copies and quiet periods leave nothing running, billed per invocation and per millisecond. It validates payloads and writes to OrderTable. StockSync reacts to table change streams to adjust InventoryStore. NightlyDigest is started by a midnight timer event and runs the same on-demand way, assembling per-tenant sales digests by querying OrderTable, fetching layouts from TemplateStore, and passing MIME text to MailRelay. Each digest query combines tenant id, date window, status list, sort key, limit and projection, with half the clauses conditional on tenant options. Current Python code builds queries two painful ways: nested dict and tuple constructors where outer-inner order hides filter intent, or six to ten setter lines on a QuerySpec temp where reviewers must read every line to see the whole request and misordered assignments slip through. Handlers are kept small, cold-start budget forbids a heavy ORM, and digest code must stay reviewable by data analysts.

state: SeatGrab sells last-minute seats for small venues. Ingress is an HTTPS edge route that emits JSON events. Business work lives in three isolated on-demand handlers hosted on Northwind Cloud on-demand compute: ReserveSeats, ReleaseHold, and PaymentConfirm. Each handler image is uploaded as a zip and the platform starts a copy only when an event or HTTP call arrives, bills for the milliseconds used, and discards the copy afterwards, so no process persists between requests. Shared state is external: a managed key-value Bookings table, a SeatInventory table, and a notification topic feeding EmailFanout. A reserve flow must check seat availability from SeatInventory, validate promo codes, compute total with fees, insert a hold row with TTL, and publish a confirmation, all as one all-or-nothing unit. The team is three backend developers in Python with no appetite for rich object graphs; each screen maps to one write operation and rules rarely change except fee percentages. They need a way to keep each handler's validation, pricing math, and persistence visible top-to-bottom with an explicit commit point, rather than spreading seat rules across interlinked classes.

state: Expensa processes expense receipts without any always-on hosts. EdgeIngress is a managed HTTP front door; POST /receipts invokes IngressFn. Writes to ReceiptBucket (object store) fire OcrExtractFn on each image. A backlog queue ReprocessQueue fires ReplayFn for bulk retries. Each Fn is shipped as an independent zip, instantiated per event with automatic concurrency, billed per millisecond of execution, and reclaimed to nothing when traffic ends, so cold start and package size matter and there is no local affinity between invocations. All three Fns must turn raw OCR text into a minor-units amount before calling LedgerWriter and PolicyStore. That conversion is five small pure unary steps in fixed order: stripWhitespace, fixOcrConfusions, parseDecimal, toMinorUnits, enforceCap. Today each Fn repeats the work as nested calls and copy-pasted temporaries, with slightly divergent order in ReplayFn causing capped values to parse differently. Product wants to add a sixth step for currency canonicalisation and to reuse subsets (first three steps) in a new SlackNotifyFn, plus unit-test each step and the full order, and pass the whole conversion as a single value to a generic retry/timeout wrapper and to an audit logger that records step timings.

state: ShopFast runs device telemetry on Kubernetes. IngestFrontdoor accepts batched POSTs from 800k phones and calls RiskScorer over gRPC for fraud scoring, then LedgerWriter for Postgres inserts. Each Pod runs two containers: the service code and a companion network container. All inbound and outbound calls pass through the companion, which enforces mTLS, applies timeouts and retries pushed from TrafficDirector, and reports traces. IngestFrontdoor sustains 18k events per sec in flash sales, while RiskScorer sustains 5k per sec due to ONNX inference and LedgerWriter sustains 3k per sec due to transactional writes. IngestFrontdoor currently pushes into a limitless in-process queue feeding sender loops. At peak the queue holds over 2M events, memory exceeds the 768Mi Pod limit causing OOM kills and lost purchases, end to end p99 exceeds 9s, and phone retries amplify the surge. Product permits answering 429 with Retry-After for phones to back off and merging repeated GPS pings per device, but purchase events must never vanish silently.

state: Retail checkout runs as five Python services: EdgeGateway, OrderService, FraudCheck, LedgerWriter and NotifyService. Each service runs in Kubernetes as a pod with two containers: the application container and a co-located traffic agent owned by the platform team. Application code never dials another service directly; it sends HTTP to http://localhost:15001/<target> and the local agent adds mTLS, retries, timeouts, load balancing and telemetry before forwarding to the destination pod agent where policy is checked again. A central TrafficDirector pushes routing tables, canary weights and auth policy to all agents, so traffic shifts need no app redeploy. Inside OrderService, OrderProcessor implements checkout business logic. It currently creates its own helpers inside its methods with InventoryClient(), FraudClient(), PostgresOrderStore() and SystemClock(). Supporting sandbox backends in staging or in-memory fakes in unit tests requires editing OrderProcessor, and its required collaborators stay invisible in its API until runtime failures. The release constraints require swapping implementations per environment and verifying logic with fakes without touching business logic, while keeping the full set of required collaborators explicit.

label: service-mesh
